https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/mark.title: Mark George KC obituary
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/mark.subtitle: Champion of social justice who represented Hillsborough families, worked with striking miners and campaigned against the death penalty
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/mark.text:
After nearly 40 years as a barrister, Mark George thought he had witnessed enough courtroom drama never to be surprised again, but he had not previously been involved in anything like the Hillsborough inquests. He led the legal team representing 22 families of Liverpool FC fans who were not only bereaved by the crush at Sheffield Wednesday’s stadium on April 15, 1989, but also suffered the trauma of their loved ones being blamed for the tragedy.
“When the forewoman confirmed that the jury were sure that the 96 [people who died] had been unlawfully killed, the families in the courtroom broke into excited shouts of joy and relief,” he wrote at the conclusion of the inquest. “For many of the families this was the holy grail: confirmation that the most senior officer on duty at Hillsborough had failed in his duty so grossly that it amounted to criminal behaviour.” The officer in question was later acquitted of manslaughter.
Those new Hillsborough inquests, which began in March 2014 and ran for two years, were the result of many years of toil by George, bringing together two of his greatest passions: football and “nailing bent coppers”, as he once said only half in jest. They involved him sifting through more than a million legal documents and watching hours of footage to uncover key evidence.
He drew parallels with the way that South Yorkshire police, the force responsible for policing that day, had also been involved in manipulating the truth during the miners’ strike five years earlier. Asked by the BBC to read through statements from more than 40 police officers who were involved in the 1984 “battle of Orgreave”, at the coking plant near Sheffield, he noted that “large parts of the officers’ statements were in almost identical language”.
George had been head of Garden Court North Chambers in Manchester since 2013. He was a champion of social justice, providing legal support to those on the margins of society, “whether it be asylum seekers, tenants in housing, workers in the workplace, or those who are prosecuted by the state”. He considered it “a hallmark of a civilised society that those people get as good representation as the state gets”.
As a defence lawyer he specialised in complex and serious criminal cases, often involving drugs, sexual assault or murder. In one especially complex case he represented the main defendant in a historical sexual assault trial at Oxford crown court, part of a series that resulted from Operation Silk, an investigation into a child sexual abuse ring in the city. There were also kidnapping and blackmail cases, including when a Chinese student in Britain unwisely boasted about his family’s wealth back home. On one occasion, when the jury were struggling to reach a verdict, George spent two weeks in the cells doing crosswords with the defendant to keep him calm.
Another high-profile case was Hanif and Khan v United Kingdom (2011) at the European Court of Human Rights. On that occasion George successfully argued that the presence of a serving police officer on the jury for the defendants’ original trial for conspiracy to supply heroin had violated their right to a fair trial, not least because police evidence was in dispute.
Much of his spare time was spent campaigning against the death penalty in the US and he was a trustee of Amicus, the London-based charity that helps to provide representation for those on death row. His first involvement in this area was in 1998, when he worked pro bono on a capital murder trial in Texas. He returned there in January 2017, spending two weeks in Houston helping his American colleagues to prepare for several capital cases.
He was particularly vexed by the long periods many prisoners spend on death row. However, he accepted the irony of maintaining that position when improvements in DNA exonerated someone who might already have been executed had the appeals process not dragged on so long.
In 2011 he helped to draft an amicus curiae brief in the case of Manuel Valle, a Cuban man who had been on death row in Florida for more than 33 years for killing a police officer, arguing that a comparison with British law showed that execution after such a lengthy period would contravene international law standards. To his dismay, the authorities went ahead with Valle’s execution by lethal injection, despite objections by the company that manufactured the drugs.
Yet the Hillsborough inquest result remained George’s most prominent success. “This is vindication of an extraordinary struggle by some extraordinary people who simply would not give up their fight for justice,” he declared. “The ramifications of this momentous day will take some time to resolve but let there be no doubt. This was victory at its sweetest. Pity it took 27 years to be achieved.”
Mark McHallam George was born in Hammersmith, west London, in 1952, the eldest of three children of John George, a solicitor in the City, and his wife, Dorothea (née McHallam), a nurse; he is survived by his siblings, Chris, an actor, and Tina, who is retired.
He was educated at a private Catholic school and contemplated going into the priesthood, but instead discovered Marx. At Jesus College, Cambridge, he read Anglo-Saxon, Norse and Celtic studies, a field in which he retained a lifelong interest. “I doubt if there are any other members of the Bar who have [that degree],” he laughed. He was fascinated by standing stones and regularly took himself on “magical history tours” to places such as Hadrian’s Wall and Sutton Hoo, trying to imagine how those fields had once looked.
Watching television coverage of “black people in the southern states of the US being beaten by racist police officers and attacked with dogs for daring to say ‘We’re human beings, we ought to be treated equally’ ” led him into the law. Such scenes made him determined to be “on the side of people who are standing up for themselves against the state”. He was called to the Bar in 1976, joined a small radical set of chambers in the Temple and took silk in 2009.
George cut his teeth on cases involving people who were arrested while protesting against the National Front in Lewisham, south London, in 1977. “Doing a series of trials for threatening behaviour, obstructing and assaulting police officers was the best advocacy training a new barrister could ask for,” he said, adding on another occasion: “It taught me that I wanted to defend, not prosecute . . . Winning cases meant that people didn’t go to prison.”
During the miners’ strike of 1984 he was engaged by the Haldane Society, a campaigning legal group. He recalled miners in Ollerton, Nottinghamshire, being given such restrictive bail conditions that it was nearly impossible for them to return to their homes. “I saw for myself the reality of what was in effect a police occupation of Ollerton as well as a number of other pit villages,” he wrote. “On one occasion when returning with my client and a mate of his from the magistrates’ court in Worksop we were stopped at a police roadblock and required to explain and justify our presence in the area.”
He went on to represent print workers, animal rights campaigners and environmentalists, including Greenpeace activists who blocked the outflow pipe of a chemical plant that was discharging unlawfully into the Irish Sea and others who bolted themselves to the road to prevent the movement of nuclear waste.
More recently he assisted dozens of people arrested in anti-fracking protests and addressed fellow lawyers demonstrating against legal aid cuts.
An early marriage to Anita (née Cave) was dissolved and he is survived by their two sons, Tom, a television and film director, and Kieran, who works in recruitment. In 1987 he met Sue Price, who worked in his chambers. “I lived happily in sin for 35 years,” she said. She also survives him with their son, Joe, a theatre lighting designer. Tom recalled being taken by his father to hear a speech by Arthur Scargill, the miners’ leader, “one of the most boring things you could ever ask a seven-year-old to do”. George was a regular blogger and tweeter and was proud of having more followers than his sons. He liked real ale and red wine, though not at the same time, and was a creature of habit. “I estimate that we ate at Pizza Express more than 300 times,” Tom said.
Undeterred by the Hillsborough tragedy, many of whose families he kept in touch with after the inquest, George remained a football fan. For several years he commuted from his home in Sheffield to London on Saturdays both to cheer Chelsea and to shout at the referee. Latterly he supported the non-league Clapton FC. He had little interest in the international game, Tom added, but “he would look out for Stenhousemuir FC’s result every week, because he liked the name”.
Mark George KC, barrister, was born on July 10, 1952. He died of prostate cancer on December 20, 2022, aged 70

image.caption: George in his chambers. He said he wanted to be “on the side of people who are standing up for themselves against the state”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: The best films of 2022
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
The streamers are challenging theatrical releases, but the big screen is fighting back. Last year, total box office revenue was up by 85 per cent compared to 2020, with No Time to Die breathing new life into cinemas. Daniel Craig’s last outing as 007 took £96.5m at the box office. Spiderman: No Way Home also bounded onto screens and passed the $1 billion mark at the international box office.
But what about this year’s releases? Our critics pick the best films of 2022 so far for this list, which we’ll be adding to regularly. Has your favourite been missed? Let us know in the comments below.
Toby Genkel, PG, 93minMaurice, who insists his name be pronounced “More-eece” in the French way, is a devious ginger cat in a fairytale world. Based on a Terry Pratchett novel, The Amazing Maurice and His Educated Rodents, it retains enough of the book’s sharpness to stand out ever so slightly from the crowd. Other cartoons have spoofed fairytales, but this one adds a few gentle digs at religion and conjures up a version of the Grim Reaper. It also offers visual zest and a lively cast of British stars on voice duties, including David Tennant, Emilia Clarke, Himesh Patel and (in the title role) Hugh Laurie.
Melissa Lesh, Trevor Frost, 15, 106minThis may be a documentary, but the plot is straight out of a sentimental movie. Harry Turner, a traumatised British veteran of the war in Afghanistan, finds a reason to go on living when he starts nurturing orphaned ocelots, hoping to reintroduce them to the wild after a period of training. The film-makers seem a bit too keen to stress the tale’s Hollywood potential. They use a polished style and highlight Turner and his conservationist girlfriend Samantha Zwicker talking about their feelings. Yet the material is indeed a strong (and sometimes painful) human-interest story — and its non-human stars, the ocelots, are compelling.
Luca Guadagnino, 18, 131minThis film is not a horror film, although there are grisly sights to rival the work of George A Romero: bloodied snouts, arterial gouts, and cadavers buzzed by flies, like the peaches in Guadagnino’s Call Me By Your Name. It is a love story, one that blooms amid the empty parking lots and convenience stores of mid-Eighties America, photographed at the violet hour, against indigo skies and mauve dusks. The result — by turns dreamy, sad, bloody and repulsive — could well be this generation’s Sid and Nancy.Read the full Bones and All review
Maria Speth, PG, 217minDieter Bachmann is a 64-year-old teacher at a provincial German school, and this documentary observes the subtle, informal approach he takes with a class of children aged between 12 and 14. They come from several countries, so Bachmann attends to their German-speaking skills while encouraging them to talk about their lives. The film has a similar unhurried style. It may run a bit too long, but that gives us more time to learn about its people and to watch them interact, which is exactly what makes it so engaging.Read the full Mr Bachmann and His Class review
Maria Schrader, 15, 128minCarey Mulligan and Zoe Kazan represent a new type of onscreen investigative sleuth, playing the two New York Times reporters who broke the Harvey Weinstein story. The film, like the reporting process, has a cumulative power and summons a hefty emotional punch thanks to some of its supporting cast.Read the full She Said review
PG, 117minThe director of Pan’s Labyrinth and The Shape of Water has turned the fairytale about a wooden boy into a stop-motion film with a strong melancholy tone. It stresses a key difference between the human race and a magical puppet: humans die. It offers a host of wonderful sights. Read the full Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio review
Bianca Stigter 12A, 69minIn 1938 an American visitor to the Polish town of Nasielsk used a 16mm camera to record everyday life. Three minutes’ worth of his images was found in 2009, so it serves as a memorial for a crowd of Jewish residents depicted in the footage, most of whom were killed in the Holocaust. This documentary r describes how the footage’s finder, Glenn Kurtz, used detective work to learn as much as he could about those people. It also muses more generally on loss, memory and the value of moving pictures. Its essential power is tremendous.Read the full Three Minutes: A Lengthening review
Aleksandre Koberidze, U, 150minIf you’re averse to whimsy, you do need to approach ’s Georgian film with caution. In low-key style, it tells of two people who fall in love at first sight but are then magically given new appearances (Ani Karseladze and Giorgi Bochorishvili), meaning they don’t recognise each other when they next meet. Around this central thread, Koberidze weaves assorted musings on life’s everyday poetry. The film does have wit and a light, airy sort of panache.Read the full What Do We See When We Look at the Sky? review
James Gray, 15, 114minJames Gray makes movies the way you’re supposed to win elections: he undersells and overperforms. Little about a Gray movie looks enticing, at a distance. His new one might be subtitled “The Year I Learnt About the Systematic Racial Inequalities of Our Supposed Meritocracy”. Only the stellar cast — Anne Hathaway, Anthony Hopkins, Jeremy Strong — might lure you into the cinema. And yet it is warm, rich and quietly engrossing. There is a raft of great performances and there is the perennially fascinating spectacle of someone growing up a little faster than they anticipated.Read the full Armageddon Time review
Charlotte Wells, 12A, 102minPaul Mescal shows his range as a divorced father on holiday with his 11-year-old daughter (Frankie Corio). It would be impressive simply as a portrait of two people, but, with its flash-forwards to the girl’s adult self, it becomes even richer. It’s a captivating debut feature from the Scottish writer-director.Read the full Aftersun review
Nathalie Alvarez Mesén, 15, 106minLiving in a remote village in Costa Rica, the middle-aged, mentally child-like Clara (Wendy Chinchilla Araya) has always had a feel for the natural world, but her religious mother won’t let her express sexual desire. In sympathy with its heroine’s increasing defiance, this film includes a brief revolt against dramatic realism. This flourish is ambitious, for sure, but I preferred the film in its general mode. Compassion and insight create all the beauty the story needs.Read the full Clara Sola review
Ryan Coogler, 12A, 161minBlack Panther: Wakanda Forever is not flawless, but it combines celebration, send-off and rambunctious legacy with the utmost respect — without allowing that respect to gum up the works and turn the whole into a wake. The film’s clearest winner is Letitia Wright. Her fierce, lithe, self-questioning presence is so unusual for a film of this size and scope, yet she pretty much shoulders this one — she’s the reed that bends and never breaks.Read the full Black Panther: Wakanda Forever review
Jafar Panahi, 12A, 106minMade by the Iranian director before he was jailed for his dissident film-making in July, this is another of the subtle yet defiant movies that have elevated him as a champion of artistic freedom. It’s fascinating as a picture of Iran and a portrait of Panahi.Read the full No Bears review
Kim Hopkins, 12A, 95minThe organisation Bradford Movie Makers, founded in 1932, today only consists of a dozen people, mainly old-timers who gather as much for companionship as for film-making. This movie is one of those docs about down-to-earth folk pottering about in loveable ways. It’s as entertaining as you wish wish, while at the same time, it doesn’t sugarcoat its rich melancholy. Read the full A Bunch of Amateurs review
Oliver Hermanus, 12A, 102minFinally Bill Nighy has found a film that is as good as he is. Everything comes together. The delicious ache of Kazuo Ishiguro’s script, the loveliness of Jamie Ramsay’s desaturated cinematography, Hermanus’s judicious direction and, above all, Nighy — mischievous and kind, amused and amusing, and self-effacing in that old-fashioned way that makes it seem a service to others.Read the full Living review
Nora Twomey, PG, 99minThis tale’s leading creature is a gentle soul. Nora Twomey’s film is aimed at younger children and gives them a rich, fantastical story with a cuddly dragon by the name of Elmer. Any viewer might be charmed by its poetic spirit and storybook visual style.Read the full My Father’s Dragon review
Li Ruijun, PG, 131minThis film shows a humble rustic couple (Renlin Wu and Hai Qing) gradually falling in love after an arranged marriage and favours tender, understated scenes that reveal the pair’s affection. Yet their efforts to create a home for themselves are brutally obstructed by state interference and this adds another dimension to the film’s quiet pathos.Read the full Return to Dust review
Billy Eichner, 15, 115minHollywood’s first gay rom-com flopped in the US. The joke is on America because the film is terrific: funny, touching and emotionally raw enough to make its characters come alive in the way of the best Judd Apatow productions. It is funny and romantic, you care for the characters and hope they pull through.Read the full Bros review
Henry Selick, 12, 106minThis comic tale of a modern American girl fighting dark forces is perhaps a bit too ambitious, but the film’s best concepts are wonderful, and the images are well designed and brought to life with punky vigour.Read the full Wendell & Wild review
Ruben Ostlund, 15, 147minAn Eat the Rich satire worthy of Borat, executed with Swiftian ruthlessness, that is probably the funniest film ever to win the Palme d’Or. Ostlund’s balance of the satirical and the picaresque would make him at home in the 18th century, you feel — he’s the son of Jonathan Swift and Henry Fielding, reborn for the age of selfies, stagflation and Sacha Baron Cohen.Read the full Triangle of Sadness review
Sacha Jenkins, 15, 104minThis documentary on the great trumpeter and singer is built around audio recordings of Armstrong talking privately about his life. It gives a potent account of his thoughts on racism.Read the full Louis Armstrong’s Black & Blues review
Martin McDonagh, 15, 114minThe In Bruges writer-director Martin McDonagh has made another film with Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson. The Banshees of Inisherin, is set in 1923 on the tiny island of Inisherin, the kind of place where you can’t fart without your neighbour hearing about it in the pub. So when Colm (Gleeson) decides that he will no longer tolerate the simplest exchange of “good mornings” with his friend, amiable Padraic (Farrell), everyone has a theory. In due time, we get a reason for the curdling of the friendship: Colm feels time slipping away and wants to devote more to his fiddle playing. He can’t be doing with any more “aimless chats with a limited man”. Push-me-pull-you forces power McDonagh’s dramas, which switch between crowd-pleasing flashes of Tarantino-like violence and Beckettian sputterings of language at its last gasp. McDonagh’s voice is so distinctive — virtuosic and filthy in the best way.Read the full The Banshees of Inisherin review
Shaunak Sen, 12A, 97minThis documentary divides its time between birdwatching and people-watching. Shot in Delhi, it features two brothers, Nadeem Shehzad and Mohammad Saud, who have set themselves up as protectors of the city’s black kites. Air pollution is an ever-greater threat to these birds of prey, so the brothers’ work gives the film a specific ecological theme. Yet this forms part of a bigger picture, an overview of the relationship between humans and their environment. Read the full All That Breathes review
Gina Prince-Bythewood, 15, 135minThis movie is simplistic but stirring stuff: a power chord of righteous, rampant sisterhood played in endless variation. It stars Viola Davis who is at the point in her career where she can dismiss someone with the blink of an eyelid. Read the full The Woman King review
Kathryn Ferguson, 15, 97minThis documentary about the singer Sinéad O’Connor tells her story from childhood to the height of fame. O’Connor speaks off camera, while the film’s archive footage shows just how big a star she was in the early 1990s. It’s a striking portrait of someone ahead of her time.Read the full Nothing Compares review
Snow Hnin Ei Hlaing, no certificate, 91minThis documentary is an informative report on life in Myanmar and a picture of a curious relationship between two people. The main setting is a women’s health clinic in the state of Rakhine. Hla, the Buddhist who runs it, is willing to treat Muslims, a policy that counts for a lot in this region, the place where the Rohingya have been genocidally persecuted. Yet she is offensively rude to her young Muslim apprentice, Nyo Nyo. As we watch Nyo Nyo’s activism, we wonder how to assess Hla’s mix of goodness and ferocity.Read the full Midwives review
Andrew Dominik, 18, 166minThis feels like an honourable attempt to render the physical and spiritual degradations of celebrity. It’s almost a horror film: Ana de Armas spooks you into what it felt like to be Monroe. For the most part, it was an out-of-body experience.Read the full Blonde review
Reginald Hudlin, 12A, 111minMade before Sidney Poitier’s death this year, this documentary features him telling his own story, speaking directly to camera. It it not only records the actor’s career, but also reminds us of the essence of his stardom: his noble charisma and smooth, regal voice. Other interviewees round out the portrait. Oprah Winfrey (one of the film’s producers), Denzel Washington and Morgan Freeman are among those who speak about his importance as a black star in Fifties, Sixties and Seventies Hollywood.Read the full Sidney review
Alex Pritz, 12A, 85minThis documentary puts us in the thick of a battle being fought in the Amazon rainforest. Its sympathies are with the Uru-eu-wau-wau, an indigenous group whose legally protected land is being invaded by would-be farmers looking to colonise it. Members of the tribe helped to make the film, but Pritz also spent time with the intruders, who state their case. As well as being informative, the movie has cinematic power. Much of the photography is dynamic, and there are moments of high drama.Read the full The Territory review
Gastón Duprat, Mariano Cohn, 15, 114minPenélope Cruz shines as an offbeat director taking on Antonio Banderas in this playful and intelligent film. It is not simply about Cruz bossing around two middle-aged men. She does that to great comic effect, but it is also a captivating film about the making of a film.Read the full Official Competition review
Chris Grubb and Luke Mellows, 105minWhen the cricket star Ben Stokes took a leave of absence to protect his mental health last year, he did an interview with the film director Sam Mendes. It forms the centrepiece of this film, which goes on to build a picture of his life and career. Stokes talks candidly but distractedly, and his exhaustion is clear in his zombie-like appearance. It gives you a good picture of its subject. Read the full Ben Stokes: Phoenix from the Ashes review
Nana Mensah, 15, 78minThis indie comic drama was written and directed by its star and shows her to be a talented, amiable storyteller. Evidently drawing on her experiences as a Ghanaian American, she plays a woman who ends up reconnecting with her family background in the Bronx after her mother’s death. Mensah brings a light touch to the usual stuff of films about modern women facing life’s hassles.Read the full Queen of Glory review
Julie Ha, Eugene Yi, 12A, 83minChol Soo Lee was a Korean-American wrongly convicted of murder in 1973. A widely supported campaign secured his release from prison in 1983, but that fight is only part of the story told in this documentary. After leaving jail, Lee felt trapped in a different way. He wanted to honour his supporters by living a useful life, but he had never been a saint and his opportunities were limited. Describing his later years, the film becomes a study of a tormented soul. It’s a potent tale. Read the full Free Chol Soo Lee review
Jordan Peele, 15, 135minThis film is all very Hitchcockian, incredibly ambitious and wholly hypnotic: the first 40 minutes, in particular, with its bluish night-time vistas of horses and clouds and flying saucers, shot in magnificent Imax widescreen by the Dutch cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema, may strike you as the most exciting piece of film-making you’ve seen all year.Read the full Nope review
Disney+, Dan Trachtenberg, 16+, 99minIn these days of the mega-franchise and multiverse, it is something of a relief to see a good, old-fashioned, down-and-dirty action movie sequel done exceedingly well. Dan Trachtenberg’s Prey is the latest addition to the Predator series, and by my count the best since Arnold Schwarzenegger. TSRead the full Prey review
Sara Dosa, PG, 98minMeeting in Strasbourg during the political ferment of the late Sixties, French volcanologists Katia and Maurice Krafft married in 1970 and spent the best part of the next two decades trotting the globe and lovingly filming rivers of lava and exploding mountaintops, at dizzying close range, before meeting their end in 1991 when a pyroclastic flow on Mount Unzen in Japan killed them alongside 41 other scientists. This is a remarkable portrait of their lives.Read the full Fire of Love review
Panah Panahi, 12A, 93minPolitical repression in Iran is a lurking theme in this drama, and it’s a subject that the writer-director, Panah Panahi, knows well. His father, the lauded film-maker Jafar Panahi, was arrested in Tehran this month and sentenced to six years in prison for “inciting unrest”. This film is the story of a family on a road trip and it is full of life. It has cinematic brio, and its best characters are distinctive, rounded versions of their archetypes.Read the full Hit the Road review
Barney Douglas, 15, 104minThe tennis player John McEnroe tells his own story in this documentary and, true to form, he gives an entertaining, intelligent and seemingly honest account of himself. There are lots of archive clips, showing him on and off court during his 1980s heyday, but the film’s director, Douglas, hasn’t left it at that. He has added scenes in which his star walks through empty New York streets at night, like a brooding private eye in a film noir. McEnroe might not be an all-time champ among sports docs, but overall this is a win.Read the full McEnroe review
Constance Meyer, 15, 95minIn this French drama a famous but miserable actor (played by Gérard Depardieu) gets to know his new security guard, a young woman (Déborah Lukumuena). Depardieu may have built himself an obnoxious public image, but he’s subtle and mesmerising in the faintly autobiographical role he has here, and Lukumuena is a match for him every step of the way. Read the full Robust review
Robert B Weide, 15, 127minAs a young man in the 1980s, the director wrote to the novelist Kurt Vonnegut to ask to make a documentary about him. The project evolved over decades and the men became friends, so the finished film is both a portrait of Vonnegut and a memoir from Weide’s point of view. It captures the author’s good-humoured personality — and something else: the passing of time and the resulting joys and pains. Vonnegut is not, of course, the only novelist to have addressed that topic, but its presence in the film is apt and poignant.Read the full Kurt Vonnegut: Unstuck in Time review
Taika Waititi, 12A, 119minDirected by Taika Waititi, the man behind Thor: Ragnarok and JoJo Rabbit, this film is a scintillatingly silly send-up of superheroes, Marvel, masculinity, Norse mythology, Shakespeare, the Thor (2011) director Kenneth Branagh and any contemporary god you care to mention. This is not just the best Marvel movie yet made, but a bona fide camp comedy classic: fast, bright, gaudy, prickly, antic and fun. It’s the silly summer movie we didn’t know we needed.Read the full Thor: Love and Thunder review
Jim Archer, PG, 90minIn this eccentric comedy Brian (David Earl) is a harebrained inventor living alone in a Welsh village who builds an autonomous robot, an ungainly creature (played by Chris Hayward) who calls himself Charles Petrescu. The story has as much scientific realism as the adventures of Wallace and Gromit, and in some ways the appeal is similar to that of the clay-model duo. The script (by the two stars) is a mixture of sweetness and silliness is wonderful.Read the full Brian and Charles review
Joseph Kosinski, 12A, 131minTom Cruise’s movie is a summer blockbuster of the old school, with rust-bucket F-14s duking it out with young pups in F-18s, all shot on celluloid rather than sketched in by computers, at the behest of a star who refuses to quit. The old dog still has it.Read the full Top Gun: Maverick review
François Ozon, 15, 103minSophie Marceau’s character in this French drama has a difficult relationship with her father (André Dussollier), and it gets no easier when, after suffering a stroke, he demands euthanasia. Based on a memoir by the writer Emmanuèle Bernheim, this is one of the more restrained films by its director. But Marceau is excellent, and the old man’s capriciousness means we can never be sure how he and the story will reach their ends.
12A, 98minConsisting of five short films by female directors, this anthology is full of cinematic flair. Marion and Ruby Grierson, the sisters of the founding figure of British documentary-making, John Grierson, have two pieces here. Marion’s Beside the Seaside (1935) is a fantastic time capsule with narration written by WH Auden. Also in the mix are Brigid Cooper’s Birth-Day (1945), which urges pregnant women to jolly well go and see a doctor, and Sarah Erulkar’s Something Nice to Eat (1967), a piece of 1960s kitsch reflecting Britain’s discovery of foreign food.Read the full The Camera is Ours: Britain’s Women Documentary Makers review
Elie Grappe, 15, 85minThis Ukrainian drama has an engrossing story. Set during the Maidan uprising of 2013-14, Elie Grappe’s movie focuses on a teenage Ukrainian gymnast (played by Anastasiia Budiashkina, herself a gymnast) forced to watch her country’s upheaval from afar. Eligible to compete for the Swiss national team, she is training with them in comfort and safety. This sparks a crisis of conscience, which she channels into gruelling gymnastic routines — the film’s vivid way of depicting the pains of exile.Read the full Olga review
Alex Camilleri, 15, 94minThis drama shows someone struggling against economic pressures in Malta. He’s a fisherman, but his luzzu (a traditional Maltese boat, painted in bright colours) is damaged, fish stocks are dwindling and EU restrictions on what he is allowed to catch aren’t helping. Needing money to cope with his baby’s health problems, he ventures into the black market. It’s a formulaic story, but its lead actor, Jesmark Scicluna, gives it heart.Read the full Luzzu review
David Fairhead and Ant Palmer, PG, 110minBrought to us by the makers of the 2018 documentary Spitfire, this is another film about a famous British warplane. David Fairhead and Ant Palmer combine old footage with handsome modern shots of a surviving aircraft in flight, and we hear from a few men who saw action in the Second World War. This sturdy account lets the veterans give their thoughts on the matter, and these — unsurprisingly — are humane and reasonable.Read the full Lancaster review
Daniel Kwan, Daniel Scheinert, 15, 139minA frazzled woman becomes a kick-ass fighter in a film that’s exhilarating and extraordinary. The directors’ creative generosity singles them out in a cinema culture that seems to be deliberately starved of fresh ideas.Read the full Everything Everywhere All at Once review
Gaspar Noé, 15, 142minThe France-based Argentine director is known for his fierce themes and avant-garde narrative methods. By these standards, his latest drama is subdued: it depicts a frail old couple (Françoise Lebrun and Dario Argento) pottering about in their flat. For all its compassion, though, it’s still a gruelling work in its account of old age’s terrors.Read the full Vortex review
Colm Bairéad, 12A, 94minSet in 1981, this film centres on a nine-year-old, Cáit (Catherine Clinch), given scant attention by her negligent father and her overstretched mother. Her life changes when she goes to stay with relatives, a middle-aged couple (Carrie Crowley and Andrew Bennett) who take care of her on their small farm. In bringing the story to a climax, the film’s writer-director shows how a well-judged movie can come near to corniness but still be deeply poignant.Read the full The Quiet Girl review
Simon Curtis, PG, 125minDownton Abbey brings out the snob in everyone, but it also confounds the snob in everyone: just when you think you’re above it all, that you can’t possibly fall for its mixture of gloss and gleam, of chocolate-box blandness and unembarrassable cliché, Maggie Smith will sink one of her withering bon mots, or someone will show someone else an unexpected kindness, and you’re a puddle again.Read the full Downton Abbey: A New Era review
Audrey Rumsby, 12A, 87minThe husband-and-wife duo Barry and Joan Grantham are old British vaudevillians who began performing together at the tail end of the variety-hall era. They bring sweet anecdotes and all-round cheeriness to documentary — along with a touch of cosmopolitan culture. Loosely structured, it relies a bit too much on its stars’ loveableness, but they do possess that quality in spades.Read the full Barry & Joan review
Andrew Dominik, 15, 105minFeaturing Nick Cave and his creative partner Warren Ellis performing songs from the albums Ghosteen and Carnage, this film is more conventional than his previous Cave movie, One More Time with Feeling. Cave describes his growing peace of mind in interviews that raise this above the average pop documentary. The performances are beautifully filmed; grandeur without pretentiousness.Read the full This Much I Know to Be True review
Marie Amiguet and Vincent Munier, 12A, 92minSnow leopards are one of the subjects of this documentary, but they aren’t easy to find, so the film is also about the search itself. Munier, a wildlife photographer, and his friend Sylvain Tesson, a travel writer, roam the Tibetan plateau, investigating and philosophising. The footage of snow leopards is brief, but you watch it with a rapturous sense of how precious it is.Read the full The Velvet Queen review
Audrey Diwan, 15, 100minIn its frank picture of how wretched life can be for women in societies that ban abortion, this Bafta-nominated French drama — set in 1963 — is an eye-opener. Audrey Diwan’s film is an in-depth portrait of a woman standing her ground. Anamaria Vartolomei gives a tender performance as a student desperately looking for a way to terminate an unwanted pregnancy — the result of her first sexual encounter.Read the full Happening review
Laura Wandel, 15, 72minIn its own way the film is an epic. Anyone who has a small child, or can remember what it was like themselves, will be able to empathise. The film grabs a tight hold and doesn’t relinquish your emotions for one second of its running time.Read the full Playground review
Giuseppe Tornatore, 15, 156minMost of the flamboyance in this documentary on the composer Ennio Morricone (who died in 2020 aged 91) comes from his music — a huge body of work known chiefly for its movie scores. The main contribution of the film’s maker, Giuseppe Tornatore (whose Cinema Paradiso has a Morricone score), is thoroughness. By the standards of arts documentaries, this one does a proper job of explaining why its subject is revered.Read the full Ennio review
Eliza Kubarska, 12A, 94minThis documentary depicts a Sherpa family offered a wage by a group of western climbers who need guides for an ascent of Kumbhakarna. As well as being one of the most challenging climbs in the Himalayas, the peak is sacred, forbidden ground for the Sherpas, yet they have noble reasons for wanting the cash. As the journey proceeds, the discussions between the guides and the tourists provide subtle human drama to complement the powerful scenery.Read the full The Wall of Shadows review
Robert Eggers, 15, 137minThis movie is a beast — a grunting, howling, gore-soaked tangle of blood, muscle and vengeance, that is incredibly violent and magisterially strange, as movies about the past really ought to be. The Northman is brutal on bodies, but it comes alive in your mind, like a spell.Read the full The Northman review
Kiro Russo, 15, 85minThis Bolivian film is pretty much Ken Loach meets David Lynch. it follows the story of a labourer (Julio César Ticona) who becomes mysteriously unwell and receives aid from a homeless shaman. Its writer-director, Kiro Russo, doesn’t always show great inspiration in the weird bits, but as a whole, they add value. Read the full The Great Movement review
Domee Shi, PG, 100minA 13-year-old girl’s growing pains give her the power of a panda in this unlikely period drama. Like most Pixar films, Turning Red has an uncanny way of drilling down into a plangent set of adult emotions while remaining nothing less than a fizzing, sherbet-filled entertainment for children. TSRead the full Turning Red review
Pierre Perifel, U, 100minA Los Angeles-based crime movie for kids, this DreamWorks animation involves a gang of roguish crooks who happen to be talking animals. Children will enjoy its all-round whizziness: the story may not be highly original, but it has more wit and coolness than the U certificate might suggest. Adults, meanwhile, will appreciate the film’s nice parallels with grown-up pulp fiction. EPRead the full The Bad Guys review
Craig Roberts, 12A, 106minMark Rylance channels Peter Sellers in this zippy story of the world’s worst golfer. With dazzled blinks, wandering gaze and halting delivery, he captures this soaringly ordinary man who has somehow found his way in front of the cameras. TSRead the full The Phantom of the Open review
David Roher, 12A, 98minFor this documentary on the anti-Putin campaigner Alexei Navalny, Daniel Roher spent time with him in Germany during a pivotal period in his life: after his recovery from the novichok poisoning he suffered in August 2020 and before his return to Russia in January 2021, when he was imprisoned. We get a sense of Navalny’s personality (confident, energetic, dry-humoured) and his family life, and we see his wily efforts to identify his poisoners.Read the full Navalny review
Juho Kuosmanen, 15, 107minSet in icy temperatures and warmed by occasional glasses of strong spirits, this Finnish drama shows a woman (Seida Harlaa) making the long train journey through Russia from Moscow to Murmansk. She has to share a compartment with a rough-hewn Russian guy (Yuriy Borisov), and the two of them slowly find they can get along. A formulaic set-up, but the director Juho Kuosmanen uses it to create all sorts of engaging scenes.Read the full Compartment No 6 review
Laura Samani, 12A, 89minThis film has an intense, straight-faced gloominess that risks being preposterous, but the success of the director in creating a fully realised world demands respect. The protagonist is a young woman (Celeste Cescutti) who is told that the soul of her stillborn — and thus unbaptised — baby is trapped in limbo. Hearing tell of a place where the dead can be resurrected for just long enough to receive baptism, she straps the little coffin to her back and sets off on a quest. It takes her through marvellous landscapes and other resonant images.Read the full Small Body review
Joachim Trier, 15, 128minPacked with soul, humour and invention, this is an Annie Hall for our age. The skill of Renate Reinsve’s beguiling, liquid performance is in how she makes inconstancy stick: she would make herself blush. She is so vividly there on screen you wonder why it isn’t performances like this that win awards, rather than the usual parade of celebrity animatronics. TSRead the full The Worst Person in the World review
Lizzie McKenzie, PG, 79minYou could argue that a hermit willing to be filmed for a documentary isn’t doing his job properly. Ken Smith, though, makes no claims to be a strict ascetic. As we learn from Lizzie McKenzie’s film, he’s a good-natured, whimsical septuagenarian who has chosen to avoid society’s hassles by living in a remote cabin in the Scottish Highlands. There are things to be learnt from his lifestyle and his appreciation of nature, but the film doesn’t preach: it’s merely a portrait of an individual. EPRead the full The Hermit of Treig review
Sebastian Meise, 18, 116minFranz Rogowski plays a gay West German who is repeatedly jailed in the years between the Second World War and his country’s decriminalisation of homosexual acts in the late 1960s. This prison drama is a believable and potent story. EPRead the full Great Freedom review
Declan McGrath and Neasa Ní Chianáin, 12A, 102minThe pupils at Holy Cross Boys’ Primary School in Belfast’s Ardoyne can be as rowdy as children anywhere, but — as this documentary shows — they have a headmaster with a rare strategy for calming them down. He teaches them philosophy. Although the film has no way to assess the long-term effect of these efforts, they are heartening to witness. EPRead the full Young Plato review
Matt Reeves, 15, 176minThis is a fully imaginative reworking of the Detective Comics era, lifted by muscular performances. Pattinson has not only the perfect jawline to play Batman, but also a reticence to his brutality, testifying to reserves of sensitivity that are teasingly drawn out by Zoë Kravitz’s Catwoman. TSRead the full The Batman review
Roger Michell, 12, 96minHow long does it take to realise that Jim Broadbent has, in Roger Michell’s The Duke, happened upon one of his greatest screen roles? About five seconds. He is brilliant in this charming, modestly scaled comedy which channels the spirit of Ealing comedies. TSRead the full The Duke review
Fred Baillif 15, 112minThis French-language drama throws us into the hubbub of life in a home for at-risk teenage girls. The narrative keeps jumping back and forth in time. This has its uses — it reminds us we shouldn’t judge people until we know what they’re going through — but it’s still a bit irritating. Even with this touch of artifice, though, the film is strongly realistic. EPRead the full La Mif review
Kenneth Branagh, 12A, 98minThis film tells the true story of how Kenneth Branagh’s family fled the Troubles. It has more of a movieish twinkle to it than the rough grit of life, and more a touch of blarney than the honesty of great autobiography, but it works: it’s probably the best film Branagh has made since his debut. TSRead the full Belfast review
Mamoru Hosoda, 12A, 121minA visual feast — even for those who aren’t anime fans. The accomplished director Mamoru Hosoda tells the story of an insecure girl who becomes a star in a world of online virtual reality. Combining science fiction, teenage angst and Beauty and the Beast, it’s exhaustingly overwrought — but it does take a refreshingly balanced view of the internet’s effect on society. EPRead the full Belle review
Paul Thomas Anderson, PG, 133minPaul Thomas Anderson’s Licorice Pizza is as perversely delicious as its title. Philip Seymour Hoffman’s son Cooper Hoffman plays 15-year-old Gary Valentine, on his way to the high-school gym to get his yearbook picture taken when he runs into the photographer’s assistant, Alana Kane (Alana Haim), who is 25, and is smitten. Their fitful, tossing and turning romance is the slender thread uniting this warm, freewheeling photo album of cockamamie adventures in the California of 1973. TSRead the full Licorice Pizza review
Philip Barantini, 15, 94minBarantini’s film is an adrenalised drama, shot in one continuous 90-minute take, about Andy (Stephen Graham), a head chef, who must in a single evening negotiate sniffy critics, celebrity drop-ins, complaining customers and prissy management, and come out in one piece. It’s compulsively hectic and Graham gives off the same electrifying charge that the young Al Pacino used to. He may be Britain’s most exciting acting talent right now. TSRead the full Boiling Point review
Asghar Farhadi, PG, 127min, on Amazon PrimeDirector Asghar Farhadi has set a high bar for himself. His film A Separation won the Oscar for best foreign language film in 2011 and he won it again for The Salesman in 2016. Like his previous work, A Hero describes a world that seems alien to us in some ways yet familiar in others. In this case, the pitfalls of social media play a part. The story is engrossing. EPRead the full A Hero review
Matthew Fifer, Kieran Mulcare, 15, 96minA story of love in the shadow of traumatic events, this indie drama features Matthew Fifer as a bisexual New Yorker haunted by his memories of being abused as a child. This may sound like an overload of misery, regardless of the fact that both of the actors’ roles are partly autobiographical. Yet the film’s realistic style makes everything convincing. EPRead the full Cicada review
Pedro Almodóvar, 15, 123minParallel Mothers is at its best when it stays in sync with its director’s own past — by giving us a colourful, passionate domestic drama. This baby-swap film about two single mothers does have moments that may seem far-fetched, but it carries them off with the help of Cruz’s performance (her eighth for Almodóvar). She gives her part incontestable, blazing life, and none of her character’s shaky decisions seems out of step with who she is. EPRead the full Parallel Mothers review
Jonas Poher Rasmussen, 15, 89minThis Oscar-nominated documentary tells the story of a gay Afghan man named Amin Nawabi who in the 1980s fled Afghanistan for Russia before finally finding sanctuary in Denmark. What distinguishes this remarkable film is its marriage of stark visuals and psychological sensitivity. National boundaries are just lines on a map, it suggests; the only worlds that matter are those inside us. TSRead the full Flee review
In cinemas, 15, 121minThis is a collection of three short tales about ordinary people and their innermost feelings. The first and the third involve the kind of piquant twists and coincidences that have become standard fare in short stories, but the middle one — in which a woman tries to seduce a male professor — is wholly unpredictable. And all three are compelling. EPRead the full Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy review
Maia Kenworthy and Elena Sánchez Bellot, 15, 83minThis inside-access documentary about the protest group Extinction Rebellion — creators of disruption as a way of demanding action on climate change — focuses on a few individuals such as the group’s zealous co-founder. It is a rewarding collection of human stories. EPRead the full Rebellion review
Will Hewitt and Austen McCowan, 15, 90minGordon Shaw is a Scottish comic-book writer and artist in his early forties who has lived for several years with a brain tumour. The film tells us that his work has given him a way of trying to cope with his condition: he has channelled his energies into an autobiographical project. As a portrait of a good man going through a hellish ordeal (with the support of his boyfriend, Shawn), this is a film of great poignancy. EPRead the full Long Live My Happy Head review
Blerta Basholli, 15, 84minThis film is a based-on-a-true-story drama about women banding together to defy sexist men by running a small business. Its setting is a village in Kosovo, and the women lost their husbands in the 1990s war. Years later, the missing men have still not been confirmed as dead, and the bereft women are expected to continue behaving as submissive wives. When they team up to produce and sell ajvar, a red-pepper condiment, the response from the village’s men is brutal. It is strong and engrossing. EPRead the full Hive review

https://www.thetimes.com/article/martin-.title: Martin Compston interview: Eight television roles are all in the line of duty
https://www.thetimes.com/article/martin-.text:
Is it the end of the line for one of the biggest names at AC-12? Martin Compston, star of Line of Duty, has hinted that the most popular drama in modern British television history may return to kill off one of its main characters — provided that the in-demand cast can find gaps in their schedules.
Compston, 38, a former footballer from Greenock, has seen his stock soar since signing up in 2012 to play DS Steve Arnott in the police corruption drama, alongside Vicky McClure and Adrian Dunbar.
He is set to star in two highly anticipated TV dramas in the coming weeks, Mayflies on BBC1 and The Rig on Amazon Prime.
Compston said: “One of the great things with Line of Duty becoming the success it has is that we’re all away doing different stuff. Trying to tie us all down at the same time isn’t easy.”
He raised the prospect of a drastic solution to the diary clash — killing off the series’s stars — but does not feel his time at AC-12 is done yet. “There could be more, I think there’s scope,” he said. “Who knows. If we do come back, then one of us has to get it sooner or later.
“I would love to work with the guys again. We’re genuinely best pals. This isn’t a reason to commission a multimillion-pound programme, but we filmed the last one in the severest of lockdowns, filming behind glass, wearing masks, nobody allowed near you.
“It wasn’t a good atmosphere for us. We wouldn’t like to finish it like that.”
Later this month Compston will star with Tony Curran and Ashley Jensen in Andrea Gibb’s adaptation of the author Andrew O’Hagan’s ode to male friendship, Mayflies.
Flip over to Amazon a week later and he’s going up in flames, doing his own stunts in The Rig, a big-budget supernatural eco-thriller.
The former Aberdeen and Greenock Morton youth footballer, whose fortunes famously changed when Ken Loach picked him to play the rough diamond lead in 2002’s Sweet Sixteen, has featured in eight TV projects since the start of the pandemic, including a Scottish travel series. It seems that not even lockdowns can keep Compston from our screens.
DS Arnott’s waistcoat has been replaced with a safety suit for Compston’s role in The Rig, in which he plays an offshore worker in an ensemble drama that is among the first to have been filmed at Jason Connery’s FirstStage Studios in Leith.
Fellow Scots Iain Glen, Mark Bonnar and Emun Elliott also feature, and the Schitt’s Creek favourite Emily Hampshire adds a splash of transatlantic glamour to the North Sea action.
“It’s going out to something like 200 countries on the day it’s released — and for something that’s filmed in Scotland, that’s amazing. Movies don’t even have that kind of reach,” Compston said.
It is, he adds, an indicator of the upward trajectory of the industry in his homeland. As a kid growing up in Inverclyde, the idea that he would one day be reading about the next Indiana Jones movie being filmed in Glasgow while sitting in Las Vegas with his American wife and toddler was the stuff of fever dreams.
“I’m still reeling at seeing Indiana Jones charging through Glasgow on horseback,” he says. “Hopefully we can keep as much of it here as we can.”
The Rig combines the industrial with the ecological and the supernatural. Think James Herbert’s The Fog on a Scottish oil platform in the Extinction Rebellion era.
“Climate change isn’t up for debate,” says Compston, who acknowledges that his lifestyle — a home on either side of an ocean — isn’t ideal. “It’s happening. But it’s a lot easier to use renewables and recycle, and it’s about the wee things that we do.”
He has spent most of the past year in Scotland, and remains finely tuned to the rise and fall of the independence wave. The recent Supreme Court ruling is like water off an offshore worker’s back.
“My opinions on that have been nailed to the mast for a long time,” he says. “That ruling hasn’t changed any of that. You can keep kicking the can down the road for as long as you like, and I think Nicola [Sturgeon] was right to make Covid the priority during the height of the pandemic. But can anyone, not just in Scotland, take any more of this Tory shower?”
His role in Mayflies springs from a particular socio-political epoch, telling a story of friendships born in the teeth of Thatcherism and the demise of heavy industry in Scotland. A story about straight, white Ayrshiremen who love their tunes and their fitba is hardly the direction of popular travel in 2022, but Compston says: “You don’t see a lot of that on screen at the minute. Racial and gender diversity in TV is a great thing. But I think it’s really important just to see this sort of friendship. It was lovely to read a script about two quite normal guys opening up to each other.”
He adds: “The west coast can be a ruthless place to grow up. You kept your dreams to yourself, because you didn’t want a slagging. But I think things are changing. Maybe it’s what comes with getting older.”
The Rig is on Amazon Prime from January 6; Mayflies is on BBC Scotland, December 27-28

https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.title: Just Stop Oil activists arrested up to seven times each during month of chaos
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.text:
Their motto was Just Stop Oil and nothing was going to stand in their way — certainly not the Metropolitan Police.
Motorists may have wondered how so many protesters were available to block bridges and roads in the capital during a month of disruption this autumn even as, day after day, the activists kept being arrested and carried away by officers.
The Times has learnt that one activist was arrested seven times during the campaign. One in five of those arrested was detained at least twice.
The Met arrested 99 protesters on two occasions, 28 on three, 25 on four and two were detained on five occasions during the group’s blockading protests between October 1 and November 4. The figures underline that despite activists being repeatedly arrested during a huge police operation that cost the taxpayer more than £5.5 million they were still able to bring London to a standstill.
Their actions, which included blockading the M25 and roads in the capital, led to some frustrated motorists dragging them out of the way. Suella Braverman, the home secretary, called on the police to introduce stronger action.
The protests were not confined to London. In March a Just Stop Oil protester stopped a Premier League match between Everton and Newcastle by tying himself to a goalpost.
In recent weeks the Met and other forces have made more arrests for public nuisance. These can be brought in the crown court, attract harsher penalties and give the authorities the ability to keep protesters in custody.
The Met confirmed that most of the arrests in the first five weeks of the protests were for the lesser offence of obstructing the highway. This attracts a fine or a maximum sentence of six months in prison and is dealt with by magistrates.
The Met said that most protesters could not be charged immediately as further investigation, such as gathering CCTV evidence or taking statements, was required. It meant that many activists were released under investigation or on bail.
Of the 755 arrests made between October 1 and November 4, a total of 155 individuals were arrested more than once. Of those, 112 have since been charged with at least one offence.
The Times previously revealed that among them were the environmental activists who threw soup at Sunflowers by Vincent van Gogh in the National Gallery on October 14. Phoebe Plummer, 21, and Anna Holland, 20, had been arrested on several occasions, including at protests in the previous seven days.
Plummer and Holland face trial for criminal damage after emptying two cans of tomato soup over the painting. Plummer had been remanded in custody over a separate charge of conspiracy to cause a public nuisance, related to disruption on the M25.
The Met said individuals arrested for a second time or more were dealt with more robustly by the force. “The repeat nature of their behaviour enables consideration of police bail conditions, or remanding in custody post charge. Of the 155 repeat offenders, 112 have since been charged with at least one offence. They will be further investigated for other offences for which they may not have yet been charged.”
This month Sir Mark Rowley, the Met commissioner, said the protest group had been “much less assertive” in its recent protests, which largely amounted to activists slowing traffic by walking along roads in the capital. He attributed this to a police crackdown that had led to dozens facing criminal charges and the alleged organisers being placed on remand in custody for conspiracy to cause a public nuisance.
The spokesman said: “We are determined to bring to justice all of those who have acted unlawfully and gone beyond protest into causing serious and criminal disruption to the public of London. To date over 12,500 officer shifts have been needed to deal with Just Stop Oil activity, and hundreds more will be needed to process all of the suspects through to a court outcome.”
The police have previously warned that they cannot always pull protesters off blockades immediately because their activities do not meet the legal threshold of serious disruption. The government is considering secondary legislation to set out a statutory definition, which could allow the police to take action earlier in a protest.
